before.exam_tip_html: In the exam, the Prologue is a powerful quotation bank for almost any question on the play. If asked about fate, conflict, or love, you can use it. Always analyse why Shakespeare reveals the ending — focus on dramatic irony and its effect on the audience. Examiners reward students who connect context (Elizabethan beliefs about fate) to the writer’s methods (the sonnet form, the word “star-cross’d”).

practice_questions.text: How does De Waal use the 1981 setting to explore ideas about racial inequality?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Perceptive analysis of how the historical setting creates meaning — links riots, sus laws, and care system to Leon’s personal story. Analyses De Waal’s methods (child narrator, juxtaposition of personal/political). Secure: Clear explanation of setting and its connection to themes of racism, with some analysis of methods. Developing: Identifies relevant contextual details but limited connection to writer’s methods. Emerging: Basic description of the setting with little analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explore how De Waal presents institutional racism in the care system.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated analysis of how systemic racism operates through apparently neutral processes — adoption panels, ‘best interests’ language, racial matching policies. Links to 1980s context. Secure: Clear analysis of how the care system fails Leon because of his race, with textual support. Developing: Identifies that Leon is treated differently but limited exploration of institutional factors. Emerging: Basic awareness that racism is present.

practice_questions.text: How does the writer use the Handsworth riots as a structural device in the novel?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses the riots as both literal backdrop and symbolic parallel — communal rage mirroring Leon’s personal rage. Discusses De Waal’s structural choices (building tension, climactic placement). Secure: Explains the connection between riots and Leon’s emotional arc with some structural analysis. Developing: Describes what happens during the riots in the novel but limited analysis. Emerging: Narrative account with little analytical focus. SPaG: 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: 'De Waal wrote My Name is Leon primarily to expose the racism of the care system.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Evaluates multiple purposes — care system racism, but also family bonds, childhood resilience, class inequality, community. Argues which is primary with evidence. Secure: Discusses care system racism and at least one other purpose with textual support. Developing: Agrees or disagrees with limited counter-argument. Emerging: Asserts a position without detailed support. SPaG: 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: How does De Waal's own background inform the authenticity of the novel?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Links De Waal’s mixed-race identity and legal career to specific narrative choices — accuracy of care proceedings, emotional truth of racial identity, insider perspective on both Black and white communities. Secure: Connects biography to the novel’s content with some specific examples. Developing: Mentions De Waal’s background but limited connection to textual choices. Emerging: Basic biographical information without analysis.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how De Waal presents the impact of Thatcher's Britain on working-class families in the novel.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Detailed analysis of how austerity, unemployment, and cuts to public services create the conditions for Carol’s breakdown and the family’s disintegration. Links economic context to emotional impact. Secure: Explains the connection between poverty and the family’s situation with some textual evidence. Developing: Identifies poverty as a factor but limited analysis of how De Waal presents it. Emerging: Basic description of the family being poor.

before.exam_tip_html: In an extract question, always link your analysis back to context. For example, if a question asks about Hyde’s appearance, connect the animalistic language to Victorian fears about degeneration and Darwin. Examiners reward answers that show understanding of why Stevenson made specific choices, not just what those choices are.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Wordsworth uses the phrase 'what man has made of man' to present the contrast between nature and humanity in 'Lines Written in Early Spring.'
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Identifies the repetition/refrain creating emphasis on human failing (1 mark)
• Explains the contrast with the natural harmony described elsewhere in the poem (1 mark)
• Analyses the word 'made' — implies deliberate construction of suffering, not accidental (1 mark)
• Links to Wordsworth's Romantic belief that nature offers moral guidance humanity has rejected (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How does Brontë present nature as an active force rather than a passive setting in 'Shall Earth no More Inspire Thee'? Support your answer with reference to the poem.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Perceptive analysis of how apostrophe gives Earth a voice and agency. Explores the reversal of typical Romantic dynamic (nature addressing human). Discusses tone — tender, reproachful, urgent. Links to Brontë's Yorkshire context.
Secure (5–6): Clear analysis of personification and apostrophe with apt references.
Developing (3–4): Some relevant points about nature speaking, with basic evidence.
Emerging (1–2): Simple identification of personification.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Wordsworth and Liz Berry present the idea of belonging to a place. You should consider the poets' methods and the ideas in each poem.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25–30): Sophisticated comparative analysis exploring how both poets tie wellbeing to a place, but through different methods — Wordsworth's philosophical argument vs Berry's dialect and physical detail. Examines form (ballad quatrains vs free verse), historical context (Romantic vs contemporary), and differing ideas of belonging.
Secure (17–24): Developed comparison with clear analytical points and relevant references.
Developing (9–16): Some comparison attempted with basic textual support.
Emerging (1–8): Limited response with minimal comparison.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Liz Berry uses sensory imagery in 'Homing' to convey the speaker's feelings about a hidden accent.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Identifies specific sensory details ('vowels ferrous as nails', 'consonants you could lick coal from') (1 mark)
• Explains how naming real dialect words makes the accent concrete rather than abstract (1 mark)
• Analyses how physical imagery conveys the speaker's love for the relative (1 mark)
• Comments on the effect of enjambment letting the lost words spill out (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How does Brontë use the concept of time in 'Shall Earth no More Inspire Thee' to explore the theme of lost connection? Refer to the poem in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Analyses how 'I've watched thee every hour' sets a long bond against the addressee's present distance. Explores the poem's urgency — 'shall' implies a critical moment of choice. Discusses how the imperatives 'Come back' and 'Return' press for a decision.
Secure (5–6): Clear analysis of temporal contrast with relevant references.
Developing (3–4): Some understanding of past/present contrast.
Emerging (1–2): Basic identification of time references.

practice_questions.text: Compare how two poems from this cluster present the idea that disconnection from nature causes human suffering.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25–30): Sophisticated comparison of two poems exploring disconnection — e.g. Wordsworth's moral grief vs Brontë's Earth's lament or Berry's grief for a silenced accent. Analyses methods (form, imagery, voice), contexts, and differing perspectives on what is lost.
Secure (17–24): Developed comparison with analytical depth.
Developing (9–16): Some comparison with basic support.
Emerging (1–8): Limited comparative response.

practice_questions.text: How does De Waal present Leon as a young carer in Part 1 of the novel?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Detailed analysis of specific actions (feeding, nappy-changing, emotional shielding) and De Waal’s methods — child perspective normalises caregiving, physical language shows love, structural positioning of Leon as protector. Secure: Clear explanation of Leon’s caring role with textual evidence and some method analysis. Developing: Identifies that Leon looks after Jake but limited analysis of how De Waal presents this. Emerging: Basic narrative description.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how De Waal uses dramatic irony in Part 1 to create emotional impact.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated analysis of the gap between Leon’s understanding and the reader’s — Carol’s ‘tiredness’ (depression), ‘medicine’ (substances), being ‘fine’ (neglect). Explains how this generates pathos and forces reader complicity. Secure: Identifies dramatic irony with examples and explains its emotional effect. Developing: Recognises that Leon doesn’t understand things the reader does, with limited examples. Emerging: Basic awareness of different perspectives.

practice_questions.text: 'Carol is a victim, not a villain.' How far do you agree with this view?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Evaluates De Waal’s nuanced presentation — Carol as failed by poverty, mental health services, absent partners. But also acknowledges the harm her neglect causes. Analyses authorial intent: De Waal wants readers to feel compassion not condemnation. Secure: Discusses both sides with textual support. Developing: Takes one position without adequate counter-argument. Emerging: Simplistic response. SPaG: 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: How does De Waal use language to present the bond between Leon and Jake?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Close analysis of tactile/physical language, promises, semantic field of warmth and protection. Links to structural purpose — establishing the bond that will be broken. Analyses how the reader is positioned to share Leon’s devastation. Secure: Identifies key language features with explanation of effect. Developing: Comments on the bond but limited language analysis. Emerging: Describes the relationship without language focus.

practice_questions.text: Explore how De Waal presents the power of social services over Leon's life.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses bureaucratic language vs. Leon’s personal language, adult conversations over his head, decisions made without consultation. Links to themes of powerlessness and institutional control. Discusses De Waal’s purpose: exposing how the system silences children. Secure: Explains power imbalance with examples. Developing: Identifies that adults make decisions for Leon. Emerging: Basic description.

practice_questions.text: How does De Waal create a sense of foreboding in Part 1?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses structural techniques — ominous details (whispered meetings, exchanged looks), escalating neglect, fragmented prose mirroring anxiety. Connects foreboding to reader engagement and dramatic irony. Secure: Identifies examples of tension-building with some analysis of methods. Developing: Recognises that the reader senses something bad will happen. Emerging: Narrative description without analytical focus.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Mundair uses the idea of a 'journey' to explore the relationship between a name and identity in 'Name Journeys.'
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Identifies the metaphor of a name as a journey from India to England (1 mark)
• Explains how this reflects the migrant experience of arrival and adaptation (1 mark)
• Analyses 'infertile English soil' or 'a stumble / that filled English mouths' (1 mark)
• Comments on the loosened ghazal form and heavy enjambment (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How does Seneviratne link her great-great-grandfather's Leeds with her own in 'A Wider View'? Support your answer with reference to the poem.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Perceptive analysis of the two time frames — 1869 and 'today' — and the images that join them ('Dark Arches', 'time, collapsing'). Explores 'he craved the comfort of a wider view'. Discusses how free verse and enjambment blur the gap between the two.
Secure (5–6): Clear analysis of past and present with apt references.
Developing (3–4): Some relevant points about the two time frames.
Emerging (1–2): Simple identification of the theme.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Mundair and Nichols present the relationship between heritage and identity. You should consider the poets' methods and the ideas in each poem.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25–30): Sophisticated comparison of a name carried into England (Mundair) and a homeland revisited (Nichols). Analyses methods (loosened ghazal vs free-verse sonnet, metaphor vs simile, personification). Explores how both poets hold pride and loss together. Links to South Asian and Guyanese contexts.
Secure (17–24): Developed comparison with clear analytical points.
Developing (9–16): Some comparison with basic textual support.
Emerging (1–8): Limited comparative response.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Nichols uses the simile 'like an heiress' to present her Guyanese childhood in 'Like an Heiress.'
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Identifies the simile that frames the coast and sky as inherited wealth (1 mark)
• Explains how 'eye-catching jewels' makes the landscape precious (1 mark)
• Analyses the turn at 'But' and the 'lone / wave of rubbish' that spoils it (1 mark)
• Comments on 'like a tourist' — she is now an outsider in her own country (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How does Mundair use language and form in 'Name Journeys' to reflect the experience of arriving in a new country? Refer to the poem in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Analyses the loosened ghazal — couplets kept, rhythm abandoned — and heavy enjambment. Explores the metaphor of Punjabi 'dislodged' onto 'infertile English soil'. Discusses the closing 'void of history and memory'. Links to Hindu references and to Mundair's Manchester childhood.
Secure (5–6): Clear analysis of form and language choices.
Developing (3–4): Some relevant points about language.
Emerging (1–2): Basic observations.

practice_questions.text: Compare how two poems from this cluster present the idea that identity is shaped by forces beyond individual choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25–30): Sophisticated comparison exploring how colonialism, family, or geography shape identity. Analyses methods, contexts, and how poets resist or embrace inherited identities. Nuanced argument about agency vs determinism.
Secure (17–24): Developed comparison with analytical depth.
Developing (9–16): Some comparison with basic support.
Emerging (1–8): Limited comparative response.

before.exam_tip_html: When writing about the opening chapters, focus on Stevenson’s use of withholding as a structural device. Examiners want to see that you understand why Stevenson delays the revelation — it builds suspense and forces the reader to share Utterson’s growing unease.

When analysing the shared sonnet (Act 1, Scene 5), always comment on form as well as language. The fact that Romeo and Juliet complete each other’s lines shows their connection. Examiners reward students who can explain why Shakespeare chose a sonnet here — it links their meeting to the Prologue (also a sonnet) and to the tradition of love poetry, while foreshadowing that their love is inseparable from their fate.

When analysing ambition, always link Macbeth’s choices to Shakespeare’s purpose. Why does Shakespeare give us “brave Macbeth” before showing his dark side? Because the tragedy is more powerful when a good man falls. In your essay, show how Shakespeare constructs Macbeth’s journey from hero to villain — the examiner wants to see that you understand the playwright’s craft, not just the plot.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Berry uses the confined space of the train carriage to present racial tension in 'On an Afternoon Train from Purley to Victoria, 1955.'
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Identifies the carriage as a microcosm of 1950s British race relations (1 mark)
• Explains how genuine warmth and casual racism sit side by side in one conversation (1 mark)
• Analyses the plain tone — making the unmeant racism seem more ordinary and disturbing (1 mark)
• Links the documentary precision (exact route, year) to testimony and truth-telling (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How does Robinson present the concept of 'home' as something that can be carried and recreated in 'A Portable Paradise'? Support your answer with reference to the poem.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Perceptive analysis of how 'white sands, green hills and fresh fish' and the imperatives 'trace', 'smell', 'hum' make paradise portable. Explores the optimism and poignancy of the title. Discusses how cultural memory sustains identity under 'stresses [that] are sustained and daily'.
Secure (5–6): Clear analysis of key imagery and the portable paradise concept.
Developing (3–4): Some relevant points about home and memory.
Emerging (1–2): Simple identification of the theme.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Berry and Robinson present the experience of displacement. You should consider the poets' methods and the ideas in each poem.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25–30): Sophisticated comparison of a single documented encounter (Berry) and an extended metaphor for carrying home (Robinson). Analyses methods: plain reportage vs sensory celebration, four conversational stanzas vs imperatives and second person. Explores contexts of Windrush and Trinidadian heritage.
Secure (17–24): Developed comparison with clear analytical points.
Developing (9–16): Some comparison with basic support.
Emerging (1–8): Limited comparative response.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Dharker uses war imagery in 'A Century Later' to present a girl's walk to school.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Identifies the allusion to Wilfred Owen's 'Anthem for Doomed Youth' (1 mark)
• Explains how 'the school-bell is a call to battle' turns a classroom into a battlefield (1 mark)
• Analyses the enjambment across the stanza break as she 'takes the bullet in the head' and 'walks on' (1 mark)
• Comments on the triumphant close: 'You cannot kill a book / or the buzzing in it' (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How does Berry use a plain, observational tone to convey both connection and casual racism in his poem? Refer to the text in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Analyses how showing rather than telling makes the woman's question about Africa land harder. Explores the warmth of 'racial brotherhood' against the joke that 'Ireland is near Lapland'. Discusses how restraint gives the poem dignity and documentary power.
Secure (5–6): Clear analysis of tone and its effects.
Developing (3–4): Some understanding of the plain tone.
Emerging (1–2): Basic observations.

practice_questions.text: Compare how two poems from this cluster present different ideas about whether migrants can ever truly 'belong' in a new place.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25–30): Sophisticated comparison exploring different routes to belonging: an unexpected conversation, a paradise carried inside you, a place claimed by defiance. Analyses methods, contexts, and the poets' differing conclusions about the possibility of belonging.
Secure (17–24): Developed comparison with analytical depth.
Developing (9–16): Some comparison attempted.
Emerging (1–8): Limited response.

practice_questions.text: How does De Waal present the character of Maureen as a source of stability for Leon?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Detailed analysis of sensory language, cultural identity provision, patience, and community-based parenting. Contrasts Maureen’s warmth with institutional coldness. Discusses limitations — she cannot reunite the brothers. Secure: Clear analysis of Maureen’s role with textual support. Developing: Describes Maureen’s kindness with limited analytical depth. Emerging: Basic description.

practice_questions.text: Explore how De Waal uses the garden as a symbol in Part 2.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses the garden as representing nurture, agency, roots, and impermanence simultaneously. Links to foster care experience and Leon’s emotional state. Discusses symbolic tension between growth and transience. Secure: Explains the garden’s symbolic meaning with examples. Developing: Identifies the garden as important but limited symbolic interpretation. Emerging: Literal description of garden scenes.

practice_questions.text: 'The separation of Leon and Jake is the novel's central injustice.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Evaluates the separation against other injustices (poverty, racism, Carol’s abandonment by services, police brutality). Argues that the separation crystallises multiple systemic failures. Analyses De Waal’s structural choices. Secure: Discusses separation as a key injustice with some comparison to others. Developing: Agrees without adequate counter-argument. Emerging: Narrative description. SPaG: 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: How does De Waal present Leon's trauma responses in Part 2?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses stealing, lying, and violence as logical trauma responses rather than moral failings. Discusses how De Waal positions the reader to sympathise through Leon’s perspective. Links to context of care system labelling ‘difficult’ children. Secure: Identifies behaviours and explains them as trauma responses. Developing: Describes Leon’s bad behaviour with some awareness of cause. Emerging: Lists behaviours without contextual understanding.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how De Waal uses the contact visits to show the gradual erosion of Leon's family bonds.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses structural diminishment (visits becoming less frequent), emotional intensity of each visit, contrast between joy and anguish. Discusses bureaucratic language and institutional control of family bonds. Secure: Explains how visits become rarer and the emotional impact. Developing: Describes the visits without structural analysis. Emerging: Basic narrative account.

practice_questions.text: How does De Waal use contrasting settings to develop themes in Part 2?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses contrasts between Carol’s chaotic home, the sterile social services offices, and Maureen’s warm home. Discusses how setting reflects emotional states and institutional values. Links to themes of belonging and identity. Secure: Identifies contrasts between settings with some thematic connection. Developing: Describes different settings. Emerging: Basic awareness of location changes.

practice_questions.text: How does De Waal use the Handsworth riots as both a literal event and a symbolic device?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated dual analysis — riots as historical event (police brutality, community response) AND as symbol (Leon’s suppressed rage erupting). Analyses the convergence of personal and political narratives at the climax. Secure: Explains both literal and symbolic functions with examples. Developing: Identifies that the riots are important but limited dual reading. Emerging: Describes what happens during the riots.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how De Waal builds tension in Part 3 of the novel.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Detailed analysis of multiple techniques — dual timelines, shortened sections, sensory escalation, restricted information. Links tension-building to reader engagement and thematic purpose. Secure: Identifies several techniques with explanation of effect. Developing: Comments on the novel becoming more exciting without detailed method analysis. Emerging: Narrative description of events.

practice_questions.text: 'The ending of My Name is Leon is hopeful.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Evaluates multiple readings — optimistic (survival, Maureen, identity), pessimistic (permanent separation, systemic victory), critical (ambiguity as political choice). Argues a personal position while acknowledging alternatives. Secure: Discusses both hopeful and pessimistic elements. Developing: Takes one position without nuance. Emerging: Simple assertion. SPaG: 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: How does De Waal connect Leon's personal story to wider political themes at the novel's climax?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses the fusion of personal grief and political anger. Leon’s epiphany connects his individual loss to systemic racism. Discusses how juxtaposition works structurally. Links to De Waal’s purpose of showing private suffering as connected to public injustice. Secure: Explains the connection between personal and political. Developing: Identifies both strands but limited integration. Emerging: Describes events without connection.

practice_questions.text: Explore how De Waal uses the child's perspective during the riots to create dramatic impact.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses restricted viewpoint — Leon doesn’t understand everything, creating tension and vulnerability. Sensory language (fire, glass, sirens) filtered through a child’s fear. Reader’s knowledge exceeds Leon’s, creating dramatic irony and anxiety for his safety. Secure: Explains how the child’s perspective creates impact with examples. Developing: Notes that Leon is a child and scared. Emerging: Describes what Leon sees.

practice_questions.text: Why is De Waal's refusal to provide a 'happy ending' significant?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses the political purpose of ambiguity — neat resolution would imply the system works; discomfort forces the reader into the position of care-experienced children. Links to De Waal’s stated purpose and real-world context. Discusses structural choices. Secure: Explains the significance of the ending with reference to purpose. Developing: Identifies the ending as sad or unfair. Emerging: Wishes it had a happy ending.

before.exam_tip_html: Act 3 is the most commonly examined section of the play. If you get an extract from this act, focus on the turning point — how Shakespeare shifts from comedy to tragedy. Always analyse Romeo’s line “O, I am fortune’s fool!” in terms of the fate vs free will debate. Examiners reward students who explore multiple interpretations rather than settling for one simple reading.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Parker uses sensory detail in 'The Jewellery Maker' to present the craftsman's life.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Identifies sensory detail from stanza 1 ('a plate-blue sky', 'heat-baked stone') (1 mark)
• Explains how the simile 'like a surgeon' and 'neat as soldiers' convey his skill (1 mark)
• Analyses the shift in stanza 3 to his wife's jewellery, 'plain' and 'worn thin' (1 mark)
• Links caesura and enjambment to the gap between his craft and his money (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How does Femi use the concept of a specific age to explore memory and identity in 'Thirteen'? Support your answer with reference to the poem.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Perceptive analysis of how the repeated age answers officers who will not believe him. Explores 'cornered', 'praying' and 'fear condenses on your lips'. Discusses the irony of the assembly officer's 'little stars'. Links to Femi's context on the North Peckham estate.
Secure (5–6): Clear analysis of age as a concept with relevant references.
Developing (3–4): Some relevant points about the police stop.
Emerging (1–2): Simple identification of theme.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Parker and Antrobus present things that are handed down between generations. You should consider the poets' methods and the ideas in each poem.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25–30): Sophisticated comparison of an inherited trade (Parker) and an inherited phrase (Antrobus). Analyses how both poets present handing down as fragile: the jeweller's wife has one thin ring; the birdsong belongs to a forest far from London. Explores free verse, caesura and couplets, and both contexts.
Secure (17–24): Developed comparison with clear analytical points.
Developing (9–16): Some comparison with basic support.
Emerging (1–8): Limited comparative response.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Antrobus uses the image of birds to explore connection and memory in 'With Birds You're Never Lonely.'
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Identifies birds as a form of communication that runs past speech (1 mark)
• Explains how the title is a phrase passed from a grandfather to a stranger to the speaker (1 mark)
• Analyses 'a silence that was not an absence' — relevant to Antrobus's deafness (1 mark)
• Comments on London's 'grey' trees without 'family' at the close (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How does Femi present the urban landscape as a complex, multi-layered environment in 'Thirteen'? Refer to the poem in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Analyses how Femi resists stereotype — the estate holds community and creativity as well as risk. Explores how the school hall of stanza 2 is set against the street of stanzas 1, 3 and 4. Discusses how the second person makes the reader stand in the boy's place.
Secure (5–6): Clear analysis of urban imagery and its effects.
Developing (3–4): Some understanding of the setting.
Emerging (1–2): Basic observations.

practice_questions.text: Compare how two poems from this cluster explore the idea that memory preserves what time would otherwise destroy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25–30): Sophisticated comparison exploring what each poem keeps (a trade, a memory of fear, a grandfather's phrase) and how each poet preserves it. Analyses poetic techniques and contexts.
Secure (17–24): Developed comparison with analytical depth.
Developing (9–16): Some comparison attempted.
Emerging (1–8): Limited response.

before.exam_tip_html: When writing about Jekyll and Hyde, avoid the common mistake of treating them as completely separate characters. Examiners want to see that you understand they are two sides of the same person. Use Jekyll’s own quotation — “man is not truly one, but truly two” — to anchor your argument.

practice_questions.text: How does De Waal present Leon as both vulnerable and resilient?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses the tension between vulnerability (child, powerless, traumatised) and resilience (resourceful, determined, protective). Discusses how De Waal uses this tension to generate reader empathy. Links to the wider theme of care-system children being punished for survival strategies. Secure: Explores both qualities with textual evidence. Developing: Identifies one quality with limited evidence. Emerging: Basic character description.

practice_questions.text: Explore how De Waal uses Jake to expose the racial hierarchy of the care system.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses Jake’s whiteness as the factor determining his ‘adoptability.’ Discusses how De Waal uses the brothers’ different fates to dramatise systemic racism without editorialising. Links to 1980s context of racial matching policies. Secure: Explains the racial difference and its consequences. Developing: Notes Jake is treated differently. Emerging: Describes the separation without racial analysis.

practice_questions.text: 'De Waal presents Carol with compassion rather than condemnation.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses De Waal’s methods — Leon’s loving memories, absence of authorial judgement, contextualisation through poverty and absent services. Acknowledges the real harm to the children while maintaining focus on systemic causes. Secure: Discusses De Waal’s sympathetic presentation with evidence. Developing: Agrees or disagrees with limited counter-argument. Emerging: Simple character description. SPaG: 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how De Waal uses Salma to explore institutional failure.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses Salma as neither villain nor hero — she represents a system that fails through process rather than malice. Discusses bureaucratic language as a form of violence. Links to De Waal’s purpose of showing how institutional racism operates through well-meaning individuals. Secure: Explains Salma’s role as system representative with examples. Developing: Describes Salma’s actions. Emerging: Basic account of what Salma does.

practice_questions.text: How does De Waal present contrasting models of care through Carol and Maureen?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses the contrast between Carol (love without capacity) and Maureen (love with stability). Neither is simple — Carol is not all bad, Maureen has limitations. Discusses De Waal’s purpose: showing that adequate care requires both love AND resources. Links to class and systemic support. Secure: Explores the contrast with textual evidence. Developing: Describes both characters as different. Emerging: Basic comparison.

practice_questions.text: How does De Waal use language to show the power dynamics between Leon and the adults who control his life?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Close analysis of contrasting registers — Leon’s physical, emotional language vs. bureaucratic euphemism. Analyses how institutional language obscures reality. Discusses the child’s position as object rather than subject of decisions. Links to power and voice. Secure: Identifies contrasting language with explanation. Developing: Notes that adults use different words. Emerging: Basic awareness of language differences.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Shelley uses the sonnet form to create a sense of political urgency in 'England in 1819.'
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Identifies the subversion of the love sonnet form for political rage (1 mark)
• Explains how the single-sentence structure creates breathless accumulation (1 mark)
• Analyses the volta — turning despair into revolutionary hope (1 mark)
• Comments on the contrast between formal control and furious content (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How does Eliot use description of the physical environment to imply criticism of Victorian society in 'In a London Drawingroom'? Support your answer with reference to the poem.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Perceptive analysis of pathetic fallacy — grey sky mirrors spiritual deadness. Explores the drawing room as both literal setting and symbol of bourgeois entrapment. Discusses gender context (woman confined to domestic sphere). Analyses how description becomes political without explicit condemnation.
Secure (5–6): Clear analysis of setting and symbolism.
Developing (3–4): Some relevant points about the gloomy description.
Emerging (1–2): Simple identification of negative imagery.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Shelley and khan present ideas about power and control. You should consider the poets' methods and the ideas in each poem.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25–30): Sophisticated comparison of overt revolution (Shelley) vs quiet, direct address (khan). Analyses how form reflects content in both: a compressed sonnet against loose free verse and single-line stanzas. Explores state power vs the power of a museum and an empire. Discusses both contexts.
Secure (17–24): Developed comparison with clear analytical points.
Developing (9–16): Some comparison with basic support.
Emerging (1–8): Limited comparative response.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how khan uses the pot in 'pot' to raise questions about looted objects and belonging.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Identifies the pot as both a museum object and a stand-in for a person (1 mark)
• Explains how the repeated 'or / did they say' makes each account sound like an excuse (1 mark)
• Analyses 'you're not really one of us' as the line that links the pot to migrant heritage (1 mark)
• Comments on the closing 'pot? / pot?' — a silence the reader must fill (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How does Shelley use imagery of death and graves in 'England in 1819' to transform political despair into revolutionary hope? Refer to the poem in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Analyses how England's corruptions are described as 'graves' — dead, buried. Explores the paradox: from graves comes a 'glorious Phantom' (revolution). Discusses how death imagery makes the current system seem already dead, making revolution inevitable rather than destructive.
Secure (5–6): Clear analysis of death/resurrection imagery.
Developing (3–4): Some understanding of the volta.
Emerging (1–2): Basic identification of imagery.

practice_questions.text: Compare how two poems from this cluster demonstrate different strategies for using poetry as political protest.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25–30): Sophisticated comparison of protest strategies: direct attack, description as critique, metaphor as resistance. Analyses how each strategy suits its poet's context (gender, era, culture). Explores effectiveness of each approach.
Secure (17–24): Developed comparison with analytical depth.
Developing (9–16): Some comparison attempted.
Emerging (1–8): Limited response.

before.exam_tip_html: When writing about character in the exam, avoid simply describing what a character does. Instead, analyse how Doyle presents them (AO2) and why (AO3). For Holmes, discuss the tension between genius and self-destruction. For Mary, explore how she both challenges and conforms to Victorian gender norms. For Small, argue whether he is a villain or a victim. The examiner rewards nuanced analysis, not plot retelling.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how one poet in the 'Worlds and Lives' cluster uses enjambment to reinforce the meaning of their poem. Support your answer with specific reference.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Identifies specific use of enjambment in a chosen poem (1 mark)
• Explains the effect: momentum, overflow, breathlessness, or flowing quality (1 mark)
• Links to the poem's theme (e.g., Shelley's enjambment = uncontainable rage; Liz Berry's = lost words spilling out) (1 mark)
• Compares with an alternative (e.g., end-stopped lines would create a different, more controlled effect) (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How does Shelley's choice of the sonnet form contribute to the political impact of 'England in 1819'? Support your answer with reference to the poem's structure.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Analyses how the love poem form is subverted for political rage. Explores the single-sentence structure creating breathless accumulation. Discusses the volta turning despair to hope. Comments on how the disciplined form contrasts with explosive content.
Secure (5–6): Clear analysis of form and structure with references.
Developing (3–4): Some relevant points about the sonnet.
Emerging (1–2): Basic identification of form.

practice_questions.text: Compare how two poets in the cluster use free verse form to reflect the themes of their poems. You should consider how form relates to meaning in each poem.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25–30): Sophisticated analysis of how free verse serves different purposes in two poems (e.g., Mundair's loosened ghazal reflecting a life between languages; Femi's second person putting the reader in the boy's place). Explores what replaces traditional structure: line breaks, spacing, rhythm variations.
Secure (17–24): Developed comparison with clear form-meaning links.
Developing (9–16): Some comparison of formal choices.
Emerging (1–8): Limited response.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how one poet in the cluster uses imagery of a specific type (visual, tactile, auditory) to create a particular effect on the reader.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Identifies specific imagery and its type (sensory category) (1 mark)
• Explains what the imagery makes the reader experience/feel (1 mark)
• Analyses how the imagery contributes to the poem's theme (1 mark)
• Comments on why this type of imagery is particularly effective for this poem's purposes (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How does the structure of one poem in the cluster reflect the experience or idea it presents? You should analyse how the poem moves from beginning to end.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Perceptive analysis of structural choices (progression, shifts, stanza arrangement) and how they mirror content. Discusses relationship between form and meaning. Analyses specific structural moments (volta, climax, resolution or lack thereof).
Secure (5–6): Clear analysis of structure with apt references.
Developing (3–4): Some relevant structural observations.
Emerging (1–2): Basic comments on structure.

practice_questions.text: Compare how two poets in the cluster use tone to communicate their attitudes towards their subject matter. Consider how tone is created through word choice and form.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25–30): Sophisticated comparison of tones (e.g., Berry's restraint vs Shelley's fury, Robinson's warmth vs Eliot's bleakness). Analyses how diction, form, and structure create tone. Explores why each poet chose their particular tonal approach and its effect on the reader.
Secure (17–24): Developed comparison with analytical depth.
Developing (9–16): Some comparison of tone.
Emerging (1–8): Limited response.

before.exam_tip_html: Questions about Utterson are really questions about Victorian values. Show how his loyalty, discretion and rationality both protect and endanger Jekyll. Link his refusal to pry to the wider theme of repression. Examiners want to see that you understand characters as vehicles for Stevenson’s ideas.

practice_questions.text: How does De Waal's choice of third-person limited narration shape the reader's experience of the novel?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses the gap between Leon’s understanding and the reader’s as a systematic technique. Discusses how this creates dramatic irony, empathy, and political critique simultaneously. Explores why third-person (not first) — the slight distance allows the reader to see patterns Leon cannot. Secure: Explains the effects of the perspective with examples. Developing: Identifies it as third person with limited analysis of effect. Emerging: Basic awareness of perspective.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how De Waal uses the novel's structure to develop meaning.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Detailed analysis of the three stages (domestic → institutional → political) as widening scope. Discusses how structure mirrors the process of political awakening. Analyses pacing within and between parts. Secure: Explains the three parts and their different functions. Developing: Describes what happens in each part. Emerging: Narrative summary.

practice_questions.text: Explore how De Waal uses sensory language to convey Leon's experience.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Close analysis of how physical/sensory detail replaces abstract thought — Leon experiences racism as a cold corridor, love as warmth, grief as physical absence. Discusses how this mirrors a child’s cognitive stage. Links to emotional impact on reader. Secure: Identifies sensory language with explanation of effect. Developing: Notes physical descriptions. Emerging: Basic quotation without analysis.

practice_questions.text: 'De Waal's use of silence is as powerful as her use of language.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses omission as a deliberate technique — Carol’s unnamed diagnosis, off-page decisions, Leon’s suppressed grief shown through absence of Jake in narration. Argues that silence generates reader engagement and mirrors Leon’s powerlessness. Secure: Discusses examples of omission with explanation. Developing: Identifies that things are left unsaid. Emerging: Limited engagement. SPaG: 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: How does De Waal use changes in pacing to create meaning?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses slow domestic rhythms (Part 1), temporal ellipsis (Part 2), and acceleration (Part 3) as structural choices reflecting Leon’s emotional state. Discusses how pacing positions the reader — monotony, loss, urgency. Secure: Identifies pacing changes with explanation. Developing: Notes the novel gets faster. Emerging: Basic observation.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how De Waal uses contrasting language registers to highlight power dynamics.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses Leon’s sensory/physical language vs. institutional euphemism. Discusses how Maureen’s warm, plain speech contrasts with Salma’s bureaucratic register. Links language to power, identity, and belonging. Explores how register shifts reveal the care system’s dehumanising processes. Secure: Identifies contrasting registers with examples. Developing: Notes different characters speak differently. Emerging: Basic awareness.

before.exam_tip_html: For the 30-mark essay on Stave 5, compare similes across staves to show structural awareness. Always link Scrooge’s actions in Stave 5 back to specific moments in Stave 1 to demonstrate understanding of the cyclical structure. Include Dickens’s social purpose — the examiner rewards answers that explain why Dickens wrote the novella, not just what happens in it. Use phrases like “Dickens intends the reader to…” or “Dickens uses this to convey his message that…”

When writing about Act 5, always address the dramatic irony of Romeo not knowing Juliet is alive. Examiners reward students who can explain why Shakespeare makes the audience watch a preventable tragedy — it forces them to feel the devastating consequences of the feud, secrecy, and impulsiveness. Compare Romeo’s elaborate death speech with Juliet’s brief, decisive action to analyse gender presentation.

practice_questions.text: How does De Waal present racism as structural rather than individual in the novel?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Distinguishes the open racism Leon meets from the racist outcomes the system produces — through adoption priorities, ‘adoptability’ criteria, and institutional blind spots. Links to 1980s context and De Waal’s purpose of exposing systemic failure. Discusses the significance of structural racism being harder to challenge than individual prejudice. Secure: Explains structural racism with examples from the text. Developing: Identifies racism in the novel. Emerging: Basic awareness that the novel is about racism.

practice_questions.text: Explore how De Waal presents different models of 'family' in the novel.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses birth family (Carol), foster family (Maureen), adoptive family (Jake’s parents), and community as family. Discusses what each model offers and lacks. Argues De Waal’s position: bonds are built through love and presence, and severing them causes permanent damage. Secure: Explores at least two models with textual support. Developing: Describes different families in the novel. Emerging: Narrative account.

practice_questions.text: 'Leon's identity is fractured by a system that has no place for complexity.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses Leon’s mixed-race identity in a binary system, his fractured sense of self after separation, and Tufty’s role in cultural anchoring. Discusses the title’s significance as a statement of selfhood. Evaluates whether the system truly has ‘no place’ or simply chooses not to accommodate. Secure: Discusses identity and belonging with evidence. Developing: Agrees without nuance. Emerging: Basic description. SPaG: 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how De Waal uses the theme of childhood and innocence to generate emotional impact.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses the tension between what Leon should be (a carefree child) and what he is forced to become (carer, fighter, survivor). Discusses how retained elements of childhood (garden, concrete thinking) make the loss more painful. Links to reader positioning and pathos. Secure: Explains how childhood is threatened with examples. Developing: Identifies that Leon shouldn’t have adult responsibilities. Emerging: Describes what Leon does.

practice_questions.text: How does De Waal present the riots as an act of resistance rather than mindless violence?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses De Waal’s contextualisation of the riots through causes (policing, poverty, racism). Discusses the parallel between communal resistance and Leon’s personal refusal to accept injustice. Explores De Waal’s balanced position — neither condoning nor condemning without acknowledging causes. Secure: Explains the riots as political with context. Developing: Notes the riots have causes. Emerging: Describes violence without analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explore how De Waal shows the intersection of race and class in the novel.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses how race and class compound each other — Carol’s poverty + Leon’s race = worst outcomes. Discusses the care system’s implicit valuation of middle-class material provision over emotional bonds. Links to Thatcher’s Britain and systemic inequality. Secure: Identifies both race and class as factors with examples. Developing: Discusses one factor in isolation. Emerging: Basic awareness of disadvantage.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how one poet in the cluster uses a specific structural choice (e.g., volta, enjambment, stanza breaks) to reinforce their poem's central theme.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Identifies a specific structural choice with a quotation or reference (1 mark)
• Explains its immediate effect on the reader (1 mark)
• Links the structural choice to the poem's central theme (1 mark)
• Evaluates why this structural choice is more effective than alternatives (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How do Berry and Robinson present different responses to the experience of being Black and British? Support your answer with reference to both poems.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Analyses Berry's record of one guarded, warm conversation vs Robinson's celebration of resilience. Explores contrasting tones (plain vs warm). Discusses how both poets use specific details but for different purposes. Links to Windrush and Trinidadian contexts.
Secure (5–6): Clear comparison with relevant references.
Developing (3–4): Some relevant comparative points.
Emerging (1–2): Basic identification of theme.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Wordsworth and Brontë present the relationship between humans and nature. You should consider the poets' methods and the ideas in each poem.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25–30): Sophisticated comparison: Wordsworth observes nature and draws moral conclusions; Brontë gives nature its own voice and agency. Analyses form (ballad vs apostrophe), perspective (human looking out vs nature looking in), and tone (meditative grief vs tender reproach). Contextualises within Romanticism.
Secure (17–24): Developed comparison with clear analytical points.
Developing (9–16): Some comparison with basic support.
Emerging (1–8): Limited comparative response.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how one poet uses a specific image or metaphor as a vehicle for exploring a larger political or social idea.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Identifies the image/metaphor and its literal meaning (1 mark)
• Explains the larger idea it represents (1 mark)
• Analyses why this particular image is effective for this idea (1 mark)
• Comments on how the poet develops the image across the poem (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How do Mundair and Seneviratne present different perspectives on heritage in Britain? Refer to both poems in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Analyses Mundair's focus on one name and one lost language vs Seneviratne's focus on an ancestor's working life. Explores how both connect heritage to a specific English city (Manchester, Leeds). Discusses methods and contexts.
Secure (5–6): Clear comparison with relevant references.
Developing (3–4): Some comparative points.
Emerging (1–2): Basic observations.

practice_questions.text: Compare how two poets in the cluster use contrasting tones to explore similar themes. You should consider how tone is created and its effect on the reader.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25–30): Sophisticated analysis of tone (e.g., Shelley's fury vs Eliot's bleakness on power; Berry's restraint vs Robinson's warmth on displacement). Analyses how diction, form, and structure create tone. Evaluates which tonal approach is more effective for the shared theme.
Secure (17–24): Developed comparison with analytical depth.
Developing (9–16): Some comparison of tone.
Emerging (1–8): Limited response.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the title of one poem in the 'Worlds and Lives' cluster encapsulates the poem's central idea or argument.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Identifies the title and explains its literal meaning (1 mark)
• Explains how the title relates to the poem's central theme (1 mark)
• Analyses specific words in the title and their connotations (1 mark)
• Comments on how the title sets up reader expectations that the poem fulfils or subverts (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How do Wordsworth and Shelley use different forms of poetry to present their political beliefs? Support your answer with reference to both poems.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Analyses Wordsworth's ballad form (democratising philosophy, folk simplicity) vs Shelley's sonnet (compressing rage, subverting love poem form). Explores how form reflects each poet's particular political message. Contextualises within Romanticism.
Secure (5–6): Clear comparison of form choices with references.
Developing (3–4): Some relevant points about form.
Emerging (1–2): Basic identification of forms.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Robinson and Liz Berry present the idea of longing for a specific place. You should consider the poets' methods and the ideas in each poem.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25–30): Sophisticated comparison of portable paradise (Robinson — recreating home through memory) vs homing instinct (Berry — reclaiming a hidden accent). Analyses sensory imagery in both, but for different purposes: Robinson's is Trinidadian memory; Berry's is Black Country dialect. Explores form, tone, and context.
Secure (17–24): Developed comparison with analytical depth.
Developing (9–16): Some comparison with basic support.
Emerging (1–8): Limited response.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how one poet uses repetition or refrain to reinforce their poem's message. Support your answer with specific reference.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Identifies specific repetition/refrain with quotation (1 mark)
• Explains the immediate effect of repetition (emphasis, rhythm, insistence) (1 mark)
• Analyses how it reinforces the poem's central argument or emotion (1 mark)
• Comments on how the repetition evolves in meaning across the poem (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How do Parker and khan use objects to explore larger ideas? Refer to both poems in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Analyses handmade jewellery as a sign of inherited skill and unequal reward vs a looted pot as a sign of empire and belonging. Explores how both poets use a concrete object to raise an abstract question. Discusses how each object's qualities map onto the idea it carries.
Secure (5–6): Clear comparison of the two objects.
Developing (3–4): Some relevant points.
Emerging (1–2): Basic identification of metaphors.

practice_questions.text: Compare how two poets in the cluster present the idea that the past continues to shape the present. You should consider the poets' methods and the ideas in each poem.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25–30): Sophisticated comparison exploring how the past persists: through a name (Mundair), through sensory memory (Femi/Robinson), through inherited phrases (Antrobus), through a great-great-grandfather's city (Seneviratne). Analyses methods for presenting time and its effects.
Secure (17–24): Developed comparison with analytical depth.
Developing (9–16): Some comparison attempted.
Emerging (1–8): Limited response.

before.exam_tip_html: When writing about supporting characters, always explain their function in the play as a whole. Examiners want to see that you understand why Shakespeare includes them. Mercutio is a foil to Romeo; Tybalt personifies the feud; the Nurse represents the failure of the adult world. Use the term “foil” in your answer — it demonstrates sophisticated literary understanding.

In the AQA exam you answer one essay question on Animal Farm, chosen from two. You write about the whole novella, closed book, with no extract printed. Always link Orwell’s methods to his purpose — examiners reward answers that explain why Orwell made particular choices, not just what happens. Use the phrase “Orwell uses [technique] to [effect] in order to [purpose]” as a structural frame.
